population.method_label: City's total, shared by actual growth
population.method_about: All of Calgary adds up to the City's own population estimate and forecast for that month, but growth is not spread evenly: each community is its 2021 Census count times one factor, plus the growth the growth model measured there (homes built since 2021). The factor spreads only what homes do not explain (more people per home since 2021, people in seniors' homes, residences and shelters, the Census undercount) over every community's 2021 count. Fast-building areas get their real growth; built-out ones grow less.

limitations: Straight-line distance, not walking distance: walking routes are longer (curved streets, rivers, rail lines, major roads), so every share is the most generous reading.
The City's inventory only: school, developer, condominium, community association and private amenities are not counted.
A transit stop is not a service level: how often buses come is not measured.
The size and condition of amenities are not measured: each playground counts as one, whatever its size.
Park crowding counts each park's whole area, natural areas and regional parks included, so homes near a very large park (Nose Hill, Fish Creek) show very high hectares per 1,000 residents.
Rental units are partly estimated: purpose-built rental buildings count as their units, from building permits or, where no permit matches, estimated from assessed value.

Children and residents are spread evenly over the homes of each community, from the population model's estimates (the 2021 Census plus modelled growth), not counted. The crowding figures will be firmed up with the 2026 Census age data in 2027.
New communities on the city's edge are naturally farther from shared facilities (recreation centres, libraries), some planned for later phases.
Community centre data needs checking: several large communities show no community centre within 800 m, which may mean community association halls are missing from the City's list.

limits: The forecast is the City's, for new communities only (its seven suburban sectors); growth in established communities (infill, redevelopment) is not in it and is not added here.

The City forecasts by sector, not by community. Each sector's figure is shared among its new communities by the homes built there in the last five years: a community just opening up (or one about to run out of land) will get more (or less) than this share.
The forecast's 2026 homes are added in full; homes built early in 2026 may already be in today's count.

Amenities in 2030 are shown two ways: today's only (nothing new opens), and today's plus what is already planned: park land zoned as reserve in new communities that is not yet a City park, and libraries, recreation centres and community centres being built and due by 2030. Planned playgrounds and new transit stops are not in any published list, so they are not added; a reserve may hold a school as well as a park.

New residents are spread over a community's homes like today's residents: new homes on the growing edge are often farther from amenities than the community's average, so 2030 crowding there may be worse than shown.
Children: the community's share of children today, applied to its new residents.

referendum.question: Question 1: Do you support the Government of Alberta taking increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels, prioritizing economic migration and giving Albertans first priority on new employment opportunities?

Question 2: Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law mandating that only Canadian citizens, permanent residents and individuals with an Alberta-approved immigration status will be eligible for provincially-funded programs, such as health care, education and other social services?

Question 3: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for social support programs as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring all individuals with a non-permanent legal immigration status to reside in Alberta for at least 12 months before qualifying for any provincially-funded social support programs?

Question 4: Assuming that all Canadian citizens and permanent residents continue to qualify for public health care and education as they do now, do you support the Government of Alberta charging a reasonable fee or premium to individuals with a non-permanent immigration status living in Alberta for their and their family's use of the health care and education systems?

Question 5: Do you support the Government of Alberta introducing a law requiring individuals to provide proof of citizenship, such as a passport, birth certificate or citizenship card, to vote in an Alberta provincial election?

Question 6: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to have provincial governments, and not the federal government, select the justices appointed to provincial King's Bench and Appeal courts?
Question 7: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to abolish the unelected federal Senate?

Question 8: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to allow provinces to opt out of federal programs that intrude on provincial jurisdiction such as health care, education and social services, without a province losing any of the associated federal funding for use in its social programs?

Question 9: Do you support the Government of Alberta working with the governments of other willing provinces to amend the Canadian Constitution to better protect provincial rights from federal interference by giving a province's laws dealing with provincial or shared areas of constitutional jurisdiction priority over federal laws when the province's laws and federal laws conflict?

Question 10: Should Alberta remain a province of Canada, or should the Government of Alberta commence the legal process required under the Canadian Constitution to hold a binding provincial referendum on whether or not Alberta should separate from Canada?

notes: Residents are counted with City's total, shared by actual growth (chosen in Settings): All of Calgary adds up to the City's own population estimate and forecast for that month, but growth is not spread evenly: each community is its 2021 Census count times one factor, plus the growth the growth model measured there (homes built since 2021). The factor spreads only what homes do not explain (more people per home since 2021, people in seniors' homes, residences and shelters, the Census undercount) over every community's 2021 count. Fast-building areas get their real growth; built-out ones grow less. The 2021 Census count is shown beside it. Rates per 1,000 residents a year use residents in the middle of each period.
Infrastructure reports are the 21 roads, water and sewer, and parks and trees service types used in the 311 equity study.
The City publishes most 311 requests at their community's centre point, not their address, so 311 is mapped by community, not by street.
Traffic incidents are the City's reported incidents with exact locations, inside the Ward 7 boundary.

Crime and disorder by community come from the Calgary Police Service community safety data (the data behind its Community Safety Dashboard), published every quarter by month. Incidents without a location are left out. The Crime Severity Index (Statistics Canada) compares Calgary with other cities each year.
